query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Controlled low‐temperature isothermal annealing applied to as‐cast eutectic HEAs will simultaneously increase both strength and ductility by refining the lamellar spacing and enhancing the interface coherence between the ductile FCC‐like phase and the hard BCC/B2 phase.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a coarse-to-intermediate lamellar microstructure comprising a soft FCC-like phase and a hard BCC/B2 phase.
generation.intervention: A precisely controlled isothermal annealing at a temperature just below the lamellar coarsening threshold (low-temperature annealing) for a set duration.
generation.conditions: Room temperature to moderate elevated temperatures (typical tensile test conditions) with thermal treatment parameters tuned to avoid excessive coarsening while achieving refinement; the alloy must remain within its microstructurally stable regime.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined eutectic lamellae with improved interface coherence and a reduced interlamellar spacing.
generation.mechanism: The low-temperature annealing induces controlled microstructural refinement. Finer lamellae act as more effective barriers to dislocation motion (increasing strength) while preserving or enhancing the connectivity of the ductile FCC-like phase (improving strain accommodation and ductility).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the treated alloy should exhibit higher yield strength along with a measurable increase in tensile ductility under identical room temperature (or moderately elevated temperature) tensile testing conditions.
generation.baseline: The unannealed, as-cast eutectic HEA with its original lamellar microstructure.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only when the annealing temperature and duration are optimized; exceeding the narrow thermal window may lead to coarsening, which could negate the improvements. Moreover, the approach relies on the stability of the dual-phase structure and might not apply if the phase balance is significantly shifted by processing variations.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal annealing temperature and time window and the quantitative degree of improvement remain to be determined experimentally, thus the magnitude of property enhancement is uncertain and may vary with specific alloy compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of as-cast eutectic HEA samples and subject them to a matrix of controlled low-temperature isothermal annealing treatments (varying both temperature and duration within a narrow window below the coarsening temperature). Conduct standardized tensile tests at room temperature on both annealed and as-cast samples. Use precise microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM/TEM) to quantify lamellar spacing and interface quality.
measurements: Lamellar spacing and interface coherence (via microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant simultaneous increase in both yield strength and ductility relative to the as-cast baseline, or if microstructural characterization indicates no refinement or degradation of interfacial coherence, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. frame.system: Eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) in their as‐solidified state with lamellar microstructures comprising a ductile FCC‐like phase and a hard BCC/B2 phase.
frame.goal: Simultaneously increase both strength and ductility for structural applications.
frame.limitation: The inherent trade‐off between strength and ductility in eutectic HEAs, where typical interventions (e.g., alloying or severe plastic deformation) improve one property at the expense of the other.
root_cause_cues: eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications
constraints: a single intervention that addresses both properties simultaneously
must specify an intervention with a clear mechanism, baseline, test conditions, prior supporting evidence, and a falsifiable experiment
frame.regime: Room temperature to moderate elevated temperatures typical for mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests) where the microstructural stability of the eutectic phases is maintained.
prior_attempts: Complex multi-step processing (e.g., combining severe plastic deformation with aging) or multi-element alloying strategies that separately target strength or ductility, but which have fallen short in achieving both improvements concurrently.
frame.understanding: A mechanism whereby microstructural refinement at the eutectic interfaces (for instance, via controlled thermal processing) enables both dispersion strengthening and an increase in ductile phase connectivity to enhance strain accommodation.

decision.trend: The earliest eutectic HEA paper (PMC4145285) showed that as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi‐based eutectic alloys naturally form a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure that offers a reasonable balance of strength and ductility. Subsequent processing—such as cold rolling—has been used to increase strength further but at the cost of ductility, and more complex multi‐step processing or additional alloying used in other HEA systems has improved one property while compromising the other. Thus, while researchers have manipulated phase volume fractions and deformation processing to boost strength, the inherent trade‐off between high strength and high ductility in eutectic HEAs remains unresolved.
decision.unsolved: The challenge is to simultaneously optimize the interlamellar architecture so that dispersion strengthening is enhanced without compromising the connectivity and strain‐accommodation capability of the ductile phase. Prior work has not found a single intervention that refines the lamellar spacing and interface coherence enough to decouple the traditional strength–ductility trade-off.
decision.why: A targeted thermal treatment just below the coarsening temperature can induce a fine-scale refinement of the eutectic lamellae. By precisely tuning the annealing temperature and time, the treatment is expected to produce a more optimal interfacial architecture that simultaneously reinforces strength (via refined barriers to dislocation motion) and improves ductility (by preserving or even enhancing the connectivity of the ductile FCC-like phase). This approach directly follows from the trend in prior processing interventions and the specific cue that microstructural refinement at the eutectic interfaces is key to resolving the strength–ductility trade-off.
